footer.disclaimer: Studet is an independent informational portal, not a university or a government body — we have no contractual relationship with the universities listed here. Programme descriptions, deadlines, fees and competition-score formulas come from each university's own publicly available sources and may be outdated or inaccurate; every programme card states whether a fact was checked by a person or extracted automatically. Always verify current information on the university's official website before making a decision — only the university makes the final admission decision.

rights.title: Your rights when applying to university
rights.intro: What Latvian law and Cabinet regulations guarantee an applicant: when rules must be published, when you can register, when the contract is signed, how fast results must be announced and how to challenge a decision.
rights.checkedNote: Prepared from the legal texts we read on likumi.lv on 20 September 2026 (Cabinet Regulation No. 846 — version of 30.12.2025; Law on Institutions of Higher Education — the version in force). This is not legal advice: the legal texts and each university's admission rules are what count.

items.title: Rules must be published by 30 November
items.text: Every year by 30 November a university must publish, on its website, the admission requirements and the start date of registration and admission for the next academic year.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 46(5); Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 3

items.title: What the rules must contain
items.text: The admission rules must state: what prior education is needed, which centralised exams must be taken, any additional requirements, when registration and admission start, the competition criteria and their weight, how the result is calculated, the competition deadline, the rights and duties of both sides, how to get information on the process, and how to appeal decisions.

items.title: An open and equal competition
items.text: Admission runs as an open and equal competition under the university's rules. A university may not give anyone an advantage that contradicts its own rules, the law or general legal principles.
items.source: Cabinet Regulation No. 846, points 2 and 8; Higher Education Law, Article 46(3)

items.title: You can register before the centralised exams
items.text: A university may open registration and admission before the centralised exams are taken. You do not have to show a school certificate or exam certificates when registering.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 46(5) and (6¹); Cabinet Regulation No. 846, points 6¹ and 6⁴ (applied from the 2026/27 academic year)

items.title: How you can register
items.text: You can register in person at the university (application plus passport or ID card) or electronically — through www.latvija.lv or the university's information system with secure authentication.

items.title: The study contract comes after documents and results
items.text: A university may sign the study contract only after you have submitted your secondary-education document and exam certificates and the competition results have been announced. After the results the university sends an invitation to sign; matriculation follows the signing of the contract.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 46(6¹) and (6²); Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 4

items.title: Results within three days
items.text: The admission committee determines and approves the competition results. They must be announced no later than three days after the competition closes.

items.title: You can ask for a refusal in writing
items.text: If the university refuses to matriculate you, you have the right to require the decision in writing (as set out in the Administrative Procedure Law).

items.title: You can appeal a decision
items.text: You can challenge the admission committee's decision on the results by submitting an application to the university's rector (at a college — the director). The rector's decision can be taken to court as set out in the Administrative Procedure Law. The deadlines for appeals are set in the university's own rules.

items.title: Exams of different levels are comparable
items.text: To compare centralised exams taken at different levels, coefficients apply: 0.75 for optimal-level exams and 0.50 for general-level exams, relative to the highest level. Exams obtained under the old system (before the new secondary-education standards) get the coefficient 0.75.

items.title: Who may skip the centralised exams
items.text: People who completed secondary education before 2004, people who completed it abroad, and people with special needs may skip the centralised exams; the mathematics exam may also be skipped by those who completed secondary education up to and including 2008. The university sets out in its rules how these people are admitted.
items.source: Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 12; Higher Education Law, Article 46(3)

items.title: A university may set additional requirements
items.text: A university may set additional requirements — special prior education, aptitude or preparation — and entrance tests to check them. These must be stated in the admission rules.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 46(4); Cabinet Regulation No. 846, points 5¹ and 13.3

items.title: If you were educated abroad
items.text: If your education document was issued abroad, attach a certificate from the Academic Information Centre (or an authorised university) saying which Latvian document it corresponds to. A foreigner must also attach proof of the language of instruction at level B2 or higher, unless an exception applies, and the university interviews them.

sources.label: Cabinet Regulation No. 846 of 10 October 2006 “Regulations on the requirements, criteria and procedure for admission to study programmes…”
Law on Institutions of Higher Education (Augstskolu likums), Article 46

glossary.title: Admission glossary
glossary.intro: Words you will meet in university admission rules and on this site. Definitions come from the laws and university rules; each one names its source.

items.definition: A programme that was found to meet the requirements of the law when its study field was evaluated.
Granting the right to deliver a particular study programme. A university may admit students to a programme only after it is licensed.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 1 clause 12 and Article 46(1)

items.definition: A person applying for admission to a study programme. The word is used in the regulations and in admission rules.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 46; Cabinet Regulation No. 846

items.definition: The university document setting the admission requirements, competition criteria and procedure. It must be published by 30 November for the next academic year.
The committee a university sets up to run admission and to determine and approve the competition results.
The open and equal selection for study places under the university's rules; its aim is to pick the best-suited candidates for the programme.
The national exam at the end of secondary school. The competition may count the mathematics, Latvian and foreign-language CEs, and other CEs you chose to take.

items.term: Level of study content (mācību satura apguves līmenis)
items.definition: The level at which a CE was taken: general, optimal or highest. You choose it yourself.
The number by which a CE result is multiplied so that exams of different levels can be compared: 1 for highest, 0.75 for optimal, 0.50 for general.

items.term: Total CE result in per cent (CE kopvērtējums procentos)
items.definition: The CE result in per cent as shown on the exam certificate. Universities multiply this number by their own coefficients.
The number a university calculates by its own rule from CE results and other criteria. Scales differ (e.g. LU — 1000 points, RSU — 100), so scores cannot be compared between universities.
items.source: Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 13.4; LU and RSU admission rules

items.definition: A mark in the secondary-education document. Universities use it in the competition for those who did not take CEs, for example people who completed school before 2004.
items.source: Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 12; LU admission rules

items.definition: A foreign-language test that can replace the CE in a foreign language in the cases set by the rules.
Requirements a university sets beyond the CEs — for example special prior education or aptitude.
A test a university may set to check that you meet its additional requirements.

Universities admit certain groups without a competition — for example olympiad prize winners. Which groups is set in each university's rules. State universities provide a budget place without competition to people who completed state defence service.
items.source: Cabinet Regulation No. 846, point 17¹; DU and LBTU admission rules

items.definition: The programmes an applicant ranks by preference in the application. The result is announced for one programme only — the highest priority where the competition was passed; the rest are no longer considered.
A study place where studies are funded from the state budget.
A study place where studies are funded by a private individual or a legal entity.
The written contract between the student and the university. It is signed after the documents are submitted and the competition results are announced.
Entering a person on the university's list of students. It takes place after the study contract is signed.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 1 clause 6 and Article 46(6²)

items.definition: The unit of study workload. A full-time student earns 60 credit points per academic year; one credit point equals 25–30 hours of study work.

items.term: Full-time and part-time studies (pilna laika, nepilna laika)
items.definition: Full-time studies correspond to 60 credit points per academic year, part-time studies to fewer than 60.
items.source: Higher Education Law, Article 1 clauses 9 and 10

items.term: Short-cycle and first-cycle programme (īsā cikla, pirmā cikla)
items.definition: The programme types you can enter with secondary education: short-cycle professional higher-education programmes and first-cycle higher-education programmes.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: How this site handles personal data: what we keep, what we don't, and what your rights are.

sections.title: In short
body: - The site has no user accounts and needs no registration.
- Exam results that you enter in the calculator or in “Where can I get in?” are calculated in your browser. They are not sent to our server and are not stored anywhere.
- We do not use tracking cookies and we show no advertising.
- Your favourites (the hearts on programmes) stay on your device only.

sections.title: Who is responsible
body: The data controller is {controller}. For questions about personal data write to: {email}.

sections.title: Visiting the site
body: When you open a page, our hosting provider automatically records technical data: your IP address, the time, the requested address and the browser type. This is done so the site works and stays secure. We do not use this data to identify anyone.
Legal basis: our legitimate interest in keeping the site secure and running (General Data Protection Regulation, Article 6(1)(f)). The retention period is set by the provider.
On a first visit we pick the language (Latvian or English) from your browser's language setting; this is not stored.

sections.title: The survey and calculators
body: - Exam results in the calculator and in “Where can I get in?” are calculated only in your browser. They are not sent to a server, not stored and not put into the page address.

- The filters you choose in the survey (field of interest, city, language and mode of study, budget places) are put into the page address so the programme list can be shown. Together with the visit they end up in the technical logs (see above), but we do not link them to a person. Exam answers from the survey are not sent to the server.

sections.title: Favourites
body: The list of programmes you mark with a heart is kept only in your browser (localStorage) and is not sent to us. You can delete it by clearing the site's data in your browser settings. This storage is needed for a feature you choose to use.

sections.title: Cookies
body: We do not use cookies for tracking. The site keeps only the favourites list in your browser (see above).

sections.title: Usage statistics
body: To understand which pages are read and how fast they load, we use PostHog analytics with servers in the European Union. It is set up as follows:
- no cookies and no data kept in the browser;
- no identification of people, no session recordings and no content of entered fields — exam results never reach analytics;
- IP addresses are not stored.
Legal basis: our legitimate interest in improving the site (Article 6(1)(f)). You can object — write to {email}.

sections.title: E-mail reminders
body: If you ask for a reminder yourself (for example about the start of admission or changes in your programme list), we store your e-mail address and what you want to be told about. We use them only for what you asked.
Legal basis: your consent (Article 6(1)(a)). You can withdraw consent at any time with the link in every e-mail or by writing to {email}; withdrawal does not affect e-mails already sent.
E-mails are sent by the provider Resend. We delete the address after you withdraw consent and no later than 12 months after the last e-mail sent.

sections.title: School pupils and young people
body: The site is mainly for school pupils and young people. In Latvia a child can give consent to an information society service from the age of 13; for a younger child the consent of a parent or legal guardian is needed (Personal Data Processing Law, Article 33).
We do not store or send the exam results you enter on the site.

sections.title: Who we share data with
body: We do not sell data and we show no advertising. Data is processed only by our service providers (processors), and only on our behalf:
- a hosting provider (running the site);
- Supabase (database with servers in the European Union; e-mail addresses, if you submit them);
- PostHog (usage statistics, servers in the European Union);
- Resend (sending e-mail).
If a provider transfers data outside the European Economic Area, it does so with safeguards approved by the European Commission, for example standard contractual clauses.

sections.title: Your rights
body: You have the right to:
- be informed about your data and access it;
- ask for it to be corrected or deleted;
- restrict processing and object to processing based on legitimate interests;
- receive your data in a portable format;
- withdraw consent at any time.
Write to {email} — we will answer within one month. If you believe your rights have been violated, you can complain to the Data State Inspectorate (Elijas iela 17, Riga, LV-1050).

sections.title: Automated decisions
body: We do not make automated decisions that affect you and we do not profile. Calculations on the site are indicative; the final admission decision is made by the university.

sections.title: Changes
body: If the policy changes we will update this page and the version date.
